explanation: Pencil 'lead' is graphite, which early users mistook for a kind of lead. Its carbon atoms form flat sheets that slide apart, while diamond locks them into a rigid framework.

claims.text: Diamond and graphite are both forms of carbon.
Diamond and graphite are not forms of lead, silicon or sulfur.
The 'lead' in pencils is graphite, which early users mistook for a kind of lead.
In graphite, carbon atoms form flat sheets that slide over each other; in diamond they form a rigid framework.

writerNotes: Self-check (CONTENT_GUIDE §9.3). lint: content:check reports no errors or warnings for this item. claims: every checkable statement is listed, and each claim with a digit, a number word, a superlative, 'only', 'first', 'invented', an etymology word or a quotation is high, as is the key of a counterintuitive item (the C26 floor). datasets: ptable records carbon as element 6 but not its forms, so checker A needs web evidence for c3; c1, c2 and c4 are textbook chemistry. rivalTest: Lead is the planted trap, because pencil cores are still called 'lead'; silicon sits below carbon in the periodic table and is the commonest mix-up; sulfur has several forms of its own, but neither diamond nor graphite. volatility: evergreen; no time words; nothing depends on knowledge newer than mid-2026. regional: the facts are taught and reported worldwide, so a player in Lagos, Mumbai, Toronto or Sydney starts level with one in London or Chicago. style: Oxford spelling, straight quotes, no en or em dashes; the explanation has 30 words. myths: screened every claim against content/reference/myths.json; no claim resembles a listed myth. mystery and encore: not applicable to a practice multiple-choice item. doubts: c3 says early users mistook graphite for lead (it was long called plumbago). I avoided the popular line that pencils 'never contained lead', because of ancient lead styluses. searches: none used.

evidence.restatement: Diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon.

evidence.restatement: Neither diamond nor graphite is a form of lead, silicon or sulfur.
Graphite was long called plumbago or black lead because early users took it for a lead ore, which is why pencil cores are still called leads.

claimResults.note: High-risk, knowledge only: no pinned dataset covers it and WebSearch was refused to this run (the shared per-turn search budget was used up), so it still needs dataset or web evidence before acceptance (§9.9 rule 3).

evidence.restatement: Graphite is stacked sheets of carbon held together by weak forces, so layers slide; diamond is a rigid three-dimensional tetrahedral network.
Diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon.
Neither is an allotrope of lead, silicon or sulfur. Silicon has a diamond-cubic crystal form but no graphite form.
Graphite was long mistaken for a lead ore and sold as black lead or plumbago, which is why pencil cores are still called lead. Werner named it graphite in 1789.

claimResults.note: High-risk claim: knowledge only in this check, so it counts only with external evidence in check A.

evidence.restatement: Graphite has stacked layers of carbon atoms that slide over each other. Diamond has a rigid tetrahedral network.

editor.reason: Both checks pass, but high-risk c3 (explanation, quotation) rests on knowledge alone in both checks, with no dataset or web evidence for it in either. No wording fix adds evidence, and stepping down the precision ladder changes claims, which needs two fresh checks (§9.2, §9.7), so it is cut. Redraft under a new id with these facts evidenced.
